passage: Creche note from Irawati, Monday. Jyoti (14 months) doesn't say words yet, but she listens closely. When I said, "Bring me your shoes," she crawled to the rack and dragged one back. When I asked, "Where's the fan?" she looked up and pointed. At clean-up I said, "Ball in the basket," and she dropped it in and clapped. I'll let her mother know, and keep giving short, one-step requests with a gesture. 😊

qa.q: What did Jyoti bring when asked for her shoes?
qa.a: She dragged one shoe back from the rack.

qa.q: What does Jyoti clapping after dropping the ball in suggest?
qa.a: She seemed pleased with herself for doing what was asked.

qa.q: Why are short requests with a gesture a good plan for Jyoti?
qa.a: They match what she can understand now and give her a clue, so she can succeed while her talking catches up.

qa.q: How might Jyoti's mother feel reading this note?
qa.a: She would likely feel reassured that Jyoti understands a lot even without words.

grounding: Shows a baby who cannot yet talk understanding and carrying out simple spoken requests.

passage: Alka is drying chillies on a mat outside their village house. Naveen, fifteen months, toddles close. "No, Naveen, don't touch. Hot," she says, shaking her head. He pulls his hand back and looks up at her face. "Go give this to Dadaji," she says, handing him a steel tumbler. He walks it carefully to his grandfather on the charpai. When Dadaji asks, "Where's the goat?" Naveen turns and points to the shed.

qa.q: Who does Naveen carry the tumbler to?
qa.a: His grandfather, Dadaji, on the charpai.

qa.q: What does Naveen looking at Alka's face after pulling his hand back suggest?
qa.a: He seemed to be checking her face to be sure he had understood, perhaps a little unsure.

qa.q: How could Alka keep building Naveen's understanding?
qa.a: She can keep using simple words with gestures and name things around the farm as they do chores.

qa.q: What would change if Alka assumed Naveen understood nothing because he can't talk yet?
qa.a: She might stop giving him small jobs, and he would miss chances to show what he understands.

grounding: Shows a toddler without speech understanding words and following simple instructions at home.

passage: At the baby song hour in a library in Oslo, Mei, thirteen months, sits on Ingrid's lap. She has no words yet. When the leader sings, "Touch your nose," Mei's finger lands on her cheek, then slides to her nose. At "Clap, clap, clap," she bangs her palms together. As they leave, Ingrid whispers, "Wave bye-bye," and Mei flaps her hand at the leader.

qa.q: Where does Mei's finger land first?
qa.a: On her cheek, before sliding to her nose.

qa.q: What does Mei's finger sliding to her nose suggest she understood?
qa.a: She seemed to understand the word "nose" and corrected her aim to match it.

qa.q: How could Ingrid build on this at home?
qa.a: She could sing the same action songs and use short everyday requests, giving Mei time to respond.

qa.q: How might the song leader see Mei's wave?
qa.a: As a sweet sign that Mei understood "bye-bye" even though she can't say it yet. 🙂

grounding: Shows a baby understanding sung and spoken instructions before she can speak.

passage: I'm Sahil, Himani's cousin. Himani is fourteen months and hardly says any words yet. But today, when her mother said, "Bring your shoes," she toddled to the door and came back with one shoe. When I asked, "Where's the cat?" she turned and pointed under the table. And when her father said, "Wave bye-bye," she waved. She understands much more than she can say.

qa.q: What did Himani bring when her mother asked for her shoes?
qa.a: She came back with one shoe.

qa.q: What does Himani's pointing under the table suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she understood the question and knew where the cat was.

qa.q: How can Himani's family support her understanding of words?
qa.a: They can keep giving simple instructions and naming things around her, and praise her when she responds.

qa.q: How does Sahil see Himani's language?
qa.a: Sahil sees that she understands much more than she can say.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing a toddler understanding words and following simple instructions before speaking.

passage:
Monday: Sarita, twelve months, looks up when her aunt Devika says, "Ball!" but doesn't move.

Wednesday: Devika says, "Give me the ball." Sarita holds it out, then pulls it back and laughs.

Saturday: Devika says, "Put the ball in the basket." Sarita crawls over, drops it in, and looks up. Devika claps. Sarita claps too.

qa.q: What did Devika ask Sarita to do on Saturday?
qa.a: She asked her to put the ball in the basket.

qa.q: What does Sarita's laugh on Wednesday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she understood the request and was playing a teasing game.

qa.q: How did Devika help Sarita learn to follow instructions?
qa.a: She used simple, clear words and gave slightly harder instructions each day.

qa.q: How might Devika feel when Sarita puts the ball in the basket?
qa.a: She probably feels delighted, seeing Sarita understand and follow her words.

grounding: Shows a toddler's understanding of spoken words and instructions growing over a week.
